meta.description: Genuine Douglas Adams. Ford Prefect says it in chapter 2 of The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (Pan Books, 1979) — not Einstein, despite the half-quote.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Time is an illusion. Lunchtime doubly so'?
meta.ogDescription: Real quote, real book: chapter 2 of The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (1979). Ford Prefect says it — and Arthur Dent deflates it in the very next line.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1952–2001 · English humorist, novelist and radio writer
answer.sourceLine: The line is Douglas Adams’s, and it sits exactly where people think it does: chapter 2 of The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, first published by Pan Books in London on 12 October 1979. One nuance worth keeping — it is a character’s line rather than Adams speaking in his own voice, and the novel deflates it on the spot, with Arthur Dent telling the speaker to send it in to the Reader’s Digest.

12 October 1979 · Pan Books, London (US edition October 1980)
Adapted from the first four “Fits” of the BBC Radio 4 series, which began 8 March 1978

source.excerpt:
“Time is an illusion. Lunchtime doubly so.”
“Very deep,” said Arthur, “you should send that in to the Reader’s Digest. They’ve got a page for people like you.”
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced page for the novel ↗ places the exact wording under “Chapter 2” of the 1979 novel, printed together with Arthur’s Reader’s Digest retort as a single exchange.

Wikipedia’s article on the novel ↗ gives the first publication as Pan Books, London, 12 October 1979, with a US edition in October 1980, and states the book was adapted from the first four parts of Adams’s radio series.

The article on the radio Primary and Secondary Phases ↗ dates “Fit the First” to BBC Radio 4 on 8 March 1978 and confirms the novel was based on the first four Fits. Its synopsis of that episode includes the pub scene, though it does not transcribe this line.

Quote Investigator has never needed to write this one up: a site-restricted search of quoteinvestigator.com for the phrase returns nothing, and Adams’s own Wikiquote page ↗ carries no Misattributed or Disputed section at all — the Hitchhiker’s material lives on the work’s page instead.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed in Wikiquote’s sourced Chapter 2 section for the 1979 novel. The reply is the half nobody quotes, and it is the half that tells you Adams knew exactly how pleased with itself the first sentence sounds.

Quoting a line this short for comment and identification is ordinary fair use, but the novel itself is not public domain and reproducing longer passages needs permission from the estate or the publisher.

author.name: Douglas Adams
author.heading: Who was Douglas Adams?
author.metaLine: 1952–2001 · English humorist, novelist and radio writer
author.bio: Douglas Adams was born in Cambridge on 11 March 1952 and died in Santa Barbara, California, on 11 May 2001, aged 49. He is best known for The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, which began as a BBC Radio 4 comedy series in 1978 and grew into a five-book “trilogy” that sold more than fourteen million copies in his lifetime. He also script-edited Doctor Who during its seventeenth season and wrote the Dirk Gently novels, and his comic voice — grand cosmic premise, resolutely mundane payoff — is the reason so many of his throwaway lines are still being quoted as philosophy.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with it anyway
misattribution.intro: The attribution is not the problem here — this really is Adams. What drifts is everything around it: who is speaking, where the sentence stops, and whose name gets attached once the joke is amputated.

items.scope: The first four words, quoted alone
items.why: Strip off the punchline and “Time is an illusion.” starts turning up over Einstein’s name — one quote database carries it that way with no source at all ↗, inviting readers to supply the citation. What Einstein actually wrote is longer and sadder: in a March 1955 letter to the family of his friend Michele Besso he said that “people like us, who believe in physics, know that the distinction between past, present, and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion” — a wry qualification about believers in physics, not a claim about physicists at large (Wikiquote, sourced ↗). The relativistic ring of Adams’s opening clause is exactly what makes the swap feel plausible.

items.who: Douglas Adams, in his own voice
items.why: Quote cards present it as an Adams aphorism about the nature of time. In the book it is dialogue — a character’s pub-philosophy, immediately punctured by Arthur Dent in the following line (Wikiquote, Chapter 2 ↗). The words are Adams’s; the sentiment is a joke he is setting up to knock down.

A comma has crept in. Film-quote listings render it “Time is an illusion. Lunchtime, doubly so.” — as here, filed under the 2005 film ↗ — while the novel text carries no comma. Tiny, but it is the tell that a copy came from the screen rather than the page.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are genuinely Douglas Adams’s. Ford Prefect says them to Arthur Dent in chapter 2 of The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, first published by Pan Books on 12 October 1979 — no comma, and with a punchline attached ↗.

context.heading: Why the joke works
lead: The gag is a bait-and-switch of scale. The first sentence borrows the cadence of physics — the sort of thing you might read about relativity and nod at — and the second one drops it straight into the pub, where the only clock that matters is the one telling you whether it is too early for a third pint. Adams sets up a cosmic proposition and lands it on a domestic one, and the two are joined by nothing but the word “time”.

The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy reached print by an unusual route. It began as a BBC Radio 4 comedy series whose first episode, “Fit the First”, was broadcast on 8 March 1978; the novel followed on 12 October 1979 ↗, adapted from the first four episodes. That is why so many of its best-known lines read like spoken comedy: most of them were written to be heard before they were written to be read.
detailsBody: Almost every reproduction of this quotation stops at “doubly so”. The novel does not. Arthur’s reply — that the remark belongs on the Reader’s Digest page for people like that — is the reason the joke is a joke rather than a fortune cookie.

Quoted whole, it is a small comic exchange about a man being pretentious in a pub. Quoted in half, it becomes the pretentious remark itself, which is a fair definition of what a quote card does to comedy.
context.pull: “Very deep,” said Arthur, “you should send that in to the Reader’s Digest.”

sourcesVerified.claim: The exact wording "Time is an illusion. Lunchtime doubly so." appears under the Chapter 2 heading of the 1979 novel, immediately followed by Arthur's reply about the Reader's Digest.
The novel was first published in London by Pan Books on 12 October 1979 (US edition October 1980) and was adapted from the first four parts of Adams's radio comedy series.
"Fit the First" was broadcast on BBC Radio 4 on 8 March 1978; the novel was based on the first four Fits; the Fit the First synopsis includes Ford taking Arthur to the pub.

Douglas Adams was born 11 March 1952 in Cambridge, England and died 11 May 2001 in Santa Barbara, California; Hitchhiker's began as a 1978 BBC radio series; he script-edited Doctor Who season 17 and wrote the Dirk Gently novels.

Einstein's sourced line reads "the distinction between past, present, and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion", from a March 1955 letter to Michele Besso's family. The page contains no "Time is an illusion. Lunchtime doubly so."
A quote database carries the bare words "Time is an illusion." attributed to Albert Einstein with no source supplied.
The comma variant "Time is an illusion. Lunchtime, doubly so." is listed as a Ford Prefect line from the 2005 film.
The quote circulates widely credited to Douglas Adams, The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, in the wording "Time is an illusion. Lunchtime doubly so."

Internet Archive holds a scanned copy of The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy by Douglas Adams (Pocket Books, ISBN 0671461494) as an access-restricted item: its collections are internetarchivebooks, delawarecountydistrictlibrary, americana and printdisabled with no inlibrary, and the lending API reports is_lendable false, is_printdisabled true, is_readable false and zero borrowable or browsable copies — so it is available to print-disabled patrons only, not general controlled digital lending.
Douglas Adams's own Wikiquote page has no Misattributed or Disputed section — only Quotes, Quotes about Adams, and External links — and does not contain this line.
